policy.criticalRule: A stage with critical diagnostic items is mastered only when its percentage reaches the mastery threshold and every critical item is correct.
policy.unlockRule: Keep mastered stages available for review, enable the first non-mastered stage as the personalized learning stage, and lock later stages.

stages.title: Web foundations
stages.focus: Structure a useful interface before adding behavior.
theory: Semantic HTML gives meaning to the document structure.
CSS controls presentation; JavaScript controls behavior and state.
Inputs, processes and outputs should be identified before implementation.
workshop: Build a semantic page with header, main, form and results area.
Explain which elements belong to structure, presentation and behavior.
Define one input → process → output flow for the project.
stages.evidence: Semantic UI shell + annotated input/process/output flow.

stages.title: Domain state & OOP
stages.focus: Represent project data with objects and valid state.
theory: A class models a responsibility; instances hold individual state.
Constructors establish required initial state.
Methods should operate on the responsibility of the object.
workshop: Create one domain class for the project.
Instantiate three objects with different valid state.
Draw the matching UML class box.
stages.evidence: Class + three instances + UML V1.

stages.title: DOM & events
stages.focus: Connect user actions to object behavior without mixing responsibilities.
theory: The DOM is the browser representation of the page.
Events connect user actions to controlled application behavior.
UI code should call domain logic instead of duplicating it.
workshop: Handle one form submit or button event.
Update the DOM from a domain result.
Prevent duplicate event behavior and document the flow.
stages.evidence: One end-to-end event → domain → DOM feature.

stages.title: Validation & persistence
stages.focus: Protect meaningful state and keep it between sessions.
theory: Validate inputs before changing domain state.
localStorage stores strings, so structured data needs serialization.
Persist only the state needed to reconstruct the application.
workshop: Reject at least two invalid inputs.
Persist a small object collection using JSON.
Reload and reconstruct the same state.
stages.evidence: Valid/invalid tests + persistence/recovery demonstration.

stages.title: Data exchange & failure states
stages.focus: Handle asynchronous data and errors explicitly.
theory: Fetch is asynchronous and can fail for network or data reasons.
Successful HTTP transport does not guarantee valid application data.
Loading, success, empty and error are distinct UI states.
workshop: Load a local or approved public JSON resource.
Render loading, success and error states.
Validate the received structure before using it.
stages.evidence: Async data flow + controlled failure state.

stages.title: Testing, accessibility & architecture
stages.focus: Make the web project defensible and maintainable.
theory: Tests cover expected, invalid and boundary behavior.
Accessible interfaces need semantic structure, labels and usable interaction.
UML and code should remain synchronized as the project changes.
workshop: Create a compact test matrix.
Run an accessibility review of labels, keyboard flow and semantics.
Refactor one responsibility and update UML.
stages.evidence: Test matrix + accessibility QA + UML V2/refactor commit.

stages.title: Python data foundations
stages.focus: Use variables, types and collections to represent observations.
theory: A dataset is a structured collection of observations and variables.
Python types affect which operations are valid.
Lists and dictionaries are useful for small structured data before Pandas.
workshop: Represent five observations with Python structures.
Identify numeric, categorical and boolean values.
Write one reusable function that summarizes a small collection.
stages.evidence: Small Python dataset + type map + reusable summary function.

stages.title: Load & inspect datasets
stages.focus: Read data and diagnose structure before calculating.
theory: CSV is text; Pandas infers a table with rows and columns.
Shape, dtypes, missing values and duplicated rows are first inspection targets.
Never compute statistics before confirming what each variable means.
workshop: Load a CSV with Pandas.
Report shape, column types, missing values and duplicates.
Write a short data dictionary.
stages.evidence: Reproducible inspection notebook + data dictionary.

stages.title: Cleaning & transformation
stages.focus: Transform data without losing traceability.
theory: Cleaning decisions must follow the meaning of the variable.
Filtering, type conversion and missing-value handling change the analytical sample.
Keep raw data separate from transformed data.
workshop: Fix one type issue and one quality issue.
Create one derived variable with an explicit rule.
Compare row counts before and after the transformation.
stages.evidence: Documented cleaning pipeline with before/after evidence.

stages.title: Descriptive statistics
stages.focus: Choose summaries that fit the variable and question.
theory: Mean, median, quartiles and dispersion answer different questions.
Outliers can affect some summaries more than others.
A statistic is useful only when interpreted in context.
workshop: Compute central tendency and dispersion for a numeric variable.
Compare mean and median and explain the difference.
Identify potential outliers using a justified rule.
stages.evidence: Statistics table + contextual interpretation.

stages.title: Visualization & evidence
stages.focus: Use plots to answer the question rather than decorate the report.
theory: Chart type depends on variable type and analytical purpose.
Axes, units and labels are part of the evidence.
A visualization should support a written claim that the data actually justifies.
workshop: Create two justified plots with Matplotlib.
Write one evidence-based statement for each plot.
Remove one misleading or unnecessary visual choice.
stages.evidence: Two labeled charts + evidence statements.

stages.title: Reproducible OOP analysis pipeline
stages.focus: Separate dataset, analysis and reporting responsibilities.
theory: Reusable analysis benefits from cohesive classes/functions.
A reproducible pipeline can run from raw input to final outputs.
Validation checks make assumptions explicit and failures visible.
workshop: Model Dataset/Analyzer/Report responsibilities.
Run the pipeline from a clean start.
Add at least three validation checks and synchronize UML.
stages.evidence: Reproducible pipeline + validation evidence + UML V2.

tracks.title: Defensive Cybersecurity
tracks.safety: Authorized defensive scope only. No external target exploitation, credential theft, persistence, malware, or destructive testing.

stages.title: Defensive scope & threat model
stages.focus: Define what is protected, what can go wrong and what testing is authorized.
theory: Security work starts with assets, threats, trust boundaries and mitigations.
CIA means confidentiality, integrity and availability.
Testing is limited to owned, sandboxed or explicitly authorized systems.
workshop: List the assets of the simulated application.
Draw one trust boundary and identify three threats.
Write the explicit authorized testing scope and exclusions.
stages.evidence: Asset list + threat model + authorized-scope statement.

stages.title: Input validation & trust boundaries
stages.focus: Treat external input as untrusted and enforce allow-list rules.
theory: Validate type, format, length and allowed values before processing.
Client-side validation improves UX but is not a security boundary.
Sensitive decisions must be enforced on the trusted/server side.
workshop: Create an allow-list validator for a safe form.
Test valid, invalid and boundary inputs.
Document which checks must remain server-side.
stages.evidence: Validator + test cases + trust-boundary explanation.

stages.title: Identity, sessions & authorization
stages.focus: Separate who a user is from what that user is allowed to do.
theory: Authentication verifies identity; authorization evaluates permissions.
Sessions carry authenticated state and require controlled lifetime/handling.
Authorization must be checked for protected operations, not merely hidden in the UI.
workshop: Model User, Role and Session objects.
Create an access matrix for at least two roles.
Simulate an authorized and denied request without attacking an external system.
stages.evidence: UML + access matrix + defensive authorization simulation.

stages.title: Least privilege, secrets & audit logging
stages.focus: Minimize permissions and preserve useful security evidence.
theory: Least privilege grants only the permissions required for a task.
Real secrets must not be committed to public repositories or browser code.
Audit logs should record relevant events without storing passwords or sensitive secrets.
workshop: Review a mock configuration for secret exposure.
Design an audit-event schema.
Show a role boundary where excessive privilege is removed.
stages.evidence: Secrets checklist + audit schema + least-privilege correction.

stages.title: Safe errors & defensive testing
stages.focus: Test misuse in controlled scenarios without leaking unnecessary information.
theory: Errors should be useful without disclosing sensitive internals.
Defensive tests cover expected misuse, invalid inputs and permission failures.
Security tests must remain inside the authorized sandbox and avoid third-party targets.
workshop: Create a defensive misuse test matrix.
Compare safe vs over-detailed error messages.
Document findings, evidence and mitigation for one simulated weakness.
stages.evidence: Authorized test matrix + safe-error review + mitigation note.

stages.title: Hardening & security review
stages.focus: Reduce exposed state, duplicated checks and ambiguous privilege before defense.
theory: Hardening removes unnecessary attack surface and centralizes policy checks.
UML should show security responsibilities and trust boundaries clearly.
A security review states mitigated risk and residual limitations rather than claiming perfect security.
workshop: Refactor one duplicated security rule into a clear service responsibility.
Update UML and threat model.
Prepare a final defensive review with risks, mitigations and residual limitations.
stages.evidence: Hardening commit + UML V2 + defensive security review.

stages.title: Coordinates, units & dimensions
stages.focus: Define a consistent geometric frame before generating solids.
theory: 3D geometry depends on a coordinate system and consistent units.
Dimensions are parameters with constraints, not arbitrary numbers.
A reproducible model states origin, axes and unit convention.
workshop: Define origin, axes and units for the project.
Create a dimension table with valid ranges.
Sketch the expected primitive using those parameters.
stages.evidence: Coordinate convention + dimension/constraint sheet.

stages.title: Primitives & geometric state
stages.focus: Represent shapes with parameters that define valid geometry.
theory: Primitives are building blocks such as boxes, cylinders and profiles.
A geometric object has state such as dimensions and position.
Constructors should reject impossible dimensions.
workshop: Create one parametric primitive class.
Instantiate three valid variants.
Reject at least one invalid dimension.
stages.evidence: Parametric primitive + valid/invalid construction tests.

stages.title: Transformations
stages.focus: Move, rotate and scale geometry predictably.
theory: Translation changes position, rotation changes orientation and scale changes size.
Transformation order can change the final result.
Transformations should use a clear coordinate convention.
workshop: Apply translation and rotation to one object.
Compare two different transformation orders.
Document the coordinate/result difference.
stages.evidence: Transformation demo + order comparison.

stages.title: Parametric OOP architecture
stages.focus: Separate geometry responsibilities from transformation and rendering logic.
theory: Classes should group cohesive geometric state and behavior.
Reusable transformation logic should not be duplicated across every shape.
UML helps reveal responsibility boundaries before the model grows.
workshop: Model Shape/Solid/Transform responsibilities.
Implement one reusable transformation behavior.
Synchronize class diagram and code.
stages.evidence: Reusable classes + UML V1.

stages.title: Composition & assemblies
stages.focus: Build larger models from reusable parts with explicit relationships.
theory: Composition models parts whose lifecycle belongs to the assembly.
Assemblies need defined reference frames and constraints.
Reusing parts is preferable to copying geometry logic.
workshop: Build an assembly from at least three reusable parts.
Explain the whole/part relationship in UML.
Change one parameter and propagate the result.
stages.evidence: Assembly model + UML relationship + live parameter change.

stages.title: Validation, export & QA
stages.focus: Verify constraints and produce a reproducible final artifact.
theory: Boundary tests catch zero, negative or incompatible dimensions.
Export is part of the pipeline and should preserve expected scale/orientation.
Final QA compares generated geometry with requirements and UML.
workshop: Create a boundary-test checklist.
Export/render the artifact with the documented convention.
Perform final requirement, geometry and architecture QA.
stages.evidence: Boundary tests + exported artifact + UML V2/QA report.

tracks.title: Robotics & Automation
tracks.safety: Simulate first. When hardware is used, respect electrical ratings, mechanical limits, emergency states and teacher-approved connections.

stages.title: Sensors, actuators & I/O
stages.focus: Identify what the system senses, decides and controls.
theory: Sensors measure or detect conditions; actuators produce controlled outputs.
Automation can be modeled as input → decision/control → output.
Every signal needs units, range and expected meaning.
workshop: Build an I/O table for the chosen automation system.
Classify each device as sensor, actuator or controller interface.
Define normal ranges for each input.
stages.evidence: I/O table + signal/range map.

stages.title: Control logic & state
stages.focus: Make decisions deterministic and define safe behavior for invalid conditions.
theory: Control logic maps current inputs/state to outputs.
A state machine defines allowed states and transitions.
Unknown or invalid input must lead to a defined safe response.
workshop: Draw a state diagram with at least three states.
Write transition rules for normal operation.
Add an explicit safe state for invalid input.
stages.evidence: State diagram + transition table + safe-state rule.

stages.title: Simulation & sensor validation
stages.focus: Validate logic with repeatable simulated readings before touching hardware.
theory: Simulation makes test sequences repeatable and reduces hardware risk.
Sensor values must be checked for type, range and plausibility.
Logs of input, state, decision and output make control bugs diagnosable.
workshop: Simulate at least six sensor readings including invalid cases.
Record expected state/output for each case.
Verify the controller enters the safe response when needed.
stages.evidence: Runnable simulation + validation/test matrix.

stages.title: OOP controller architecture
stages.focus: Separate Sensor, Controller, Actuator and System responsibilities.
theory: Hardware interfaces and decision logic should not be one monolithic block.
Classes can encapsulate sensor reading, control policy and actuator commands.
The controller should depend on clear interfaces so simulation and hardware can share logic.
workshop: Create Sensor/Controller/Actuator/System classes or interfaces.
Run the same controller against simulated devices.
Draw matching UML V1.
stages.evidence: Class-based controller + simulation + UML V1.

stages.title: Fail-safe state machine
stages.focus: Handle transitions, timeouts and abnormal readings without unsafe output.
theory: Fail-safe behavior moves the system toward a defined safer state when assumptions fail.
Timeouts and impossible readings are control events, not values to ignore.
Actuator limits must be enforced before commands reach hardware.
workshop: Add timeout/invalid-reading transitions.
Clamp or reject an out-of-range actuator command.
Test recovery from the fail-safe state using a documented rule.
stages.evidence: Fail-safe implementation + boundary tests + transition evidence.

stages.title: Hardware integration & system QA
stages.focus: Connect only after simulation passes, then verify electrical and behavioral limits.
theory: Voltage, current, polarity and mechanical limits must follow device documentation.
Integration testing uses known input sequences and expected outputs.
A safe demonstration includes a stop/neutral condition and a way to recover from faults.
workshop: Complete a teacher-approved hardware checklist or advanced simulation equivalent.
Run an integration test matrix.
Update UML and demonstrate normal + safe-stop behavior.
stages.evidence: Safety checklist + integrated prototype/simulation + UML V2 + demo.
